modern:
Anything is better than the dead calm of indifference. Our souls may wisely long for the north wind of trouble, if that is the only thing God will use to draw out the perfume of our graces. As long as it can’t be said, “The Lord was not in the wind,” we won’t shrink from the most wintry blast that ever blew on plants of grace. Didn’t the bride in this verse humbly submit to her Beloved’s rebukes? She only begged him to send his grace in some form, and laid down no conditions about the way it should come. Didn’t she, like us, grow so tired of deadness and unholy calm that she longed for anything at all that would rouse her to action? Yet she wants the warm south wind of comfort too: the smiles of God’s love, the joy of the Redeemer’s presence. These are often wonderfully effective at stirring up our sluggish life. She wants one or the other, or both, as long as she can delight her Beloved with the spices of her garden. She can’t bear to be useless, and neither can we.

How cheering it is to think that Jesus can find comfort in our poor, feeble graces! Can it be? It seems far too good to be true. We may well welcome trial, or even death itself, if it helps us make Immanuel’s heart glad. Oh, that our hearts were crushed to pieces, if only by that bruising our sweet Lord Jesus could be glorified! Graces that are never exercised are like sweet perfumes sleeping in the cups of the flowers. The great Gardener, in his wisdom, overrules different and even opposite causes to produce the one result he wants. He makes both trouble and comfort draw out the pleasing fragrance of faith, love, patience, hope, surrender, joy and the other lovely flowers of the garden. May we know by sweet experience what this means.

modern:
As all the rivers run into the sea, so all delights meet in our Beloved. The glance of his eyes outshines the sun. The beauty of his face is lovelier than the choicest flowers. No fragrance is like the breath of his mouth. Gems from the mine and pearls from the sea are worthless when measured against his preciousness. Peter tells us that Jesus is precious, but he didn’t and couldn’t tell us *how* precious, and none of us could work out the value of God’s gift that is too great for words. Words can’t express how precious the Lord Jesus is to his people, or fully say how essential he is to their satisfaction and happiness.

Believer, haven’t you found a bitter famine in the middle of plenty when your Lord has been absent? The sun was shining, but Christ had hidden himself, and the whole world was black to you. Or it was night, and since the bright morning star was gone, no other star could give you even a ray of light. What a howling wilderness this world is without our Lord! If he once hides himself from us, the flowers of our garden wither, our pleasant fruit decays, the birds stop singing and a storm overturns our hopes. All the candles on earth can’t make daylight if the Sun of Righteousness is eclipsed. He is the soul of our soul, the light of our light, the life of our life. Dear reader, what would you do in the world without him, when you wake up and look ahead to the day’s battle? What would you do at night, when you come home worn out and tired, if there were no door of fellowship between you and Christ? Blessed be his name, he won’t let us try life without him, because Jesus never leaves his own. Still, let the thought of *what life would be without him* make him all the more precious to you.

modern: We’re fighting a great war against the Philistines of evil. *Every weapon within reach must be used.* Preaching, teaching, praying, giving: all of it must be brought into action, and talents that were thought too humble to be of service must be put to work now. Plowshare and axe and pick may all be useful for killing Philistines. Rough tools can deal hard blows, and the killing doesn’t need to be done elegantly, as long as it’s done effectively. Every moment of time, convenient or not; every scrap of ability, trained or untrained; every opportunity, favorable or unfavorable, must be used, because our enemies are many and our forces few.

*Most of our tools need sharpening.* We need quick perception, tact, energy and promptness: in a word, to be fully fitted for the Lord’s work. Practical common sense is very rare among those who run Christian enterprises. We could learn from our enemies if we wanted to, and so *make the Philistines sharpen our weapons*. This morning let’s notice enough to sharpen our zeal for today, with the help of the Holy Spirit. Look at the energy of the Roman Catholics, how they travel land and sea to make one convert. Are they to have all the earnestness to themselves? Look at the pagan worshipers, and the tortures they endure in the service of their idols! Are they the only ones to show patience and self-sacrifice? Look at the prince of darkness: how persistent in his efforts, how shameless in his attempts, how daring in his plans, how thoughtful in his plots, how energetic in everything! The devils are united as one man in their wicked rebellion, while we believers in Jesus are divided in our service of God and hardly ever work together in agreement. Oh, that we might learn from Satan’s hellish hard work to go about like good Samaritans, looking for people we can bless!

modern:
The apostle Paul thought it a great privilege to be allowed to preach the gospel. He didn’t see his calling as drudgery. He took it up with intense delight. Yet while Paul was so thankful for his work, his success in it humbled him greatly. The fuller a ship becomes, the deeper it sinks in the water. Idle people may have a fond, high opinion of their abilities, because they’ve never been tested, but the earnest worker soon learns how weak he is. If you want humility, *try hard work*. If you want to know your own nothingness, try some great thing for Jesus. If you want to feel how completely powerless you are apart from the living God, try especially the great work of proclaiming the unsearchable riches of Christ, and you’ll know as never before what a weak, unworthy thing you are.

But though the apostle knew and admitted his weakness like this, he was never confused about the *subject* of his preaching. From his first sermon to his last, Paul preached Christ and nothing but Christ. He lifted up the cross and praised the Son of God who bled on it. Follow his example in all your own efforts to spread the good news of salvation, and let “Christ and him crucified” be your theme again and again. The Christian should be like those lovely spring flowers that open their golden cups when the sun is shining, as if to say, “Fill us with your beams!” but close them and droop their heads when the sun goes behind a cloud. In the same way the Christian should feel the sweet influence of Jesus. Jesus must be his sun, and he must be the flower that gives itself to the Sun of Righteousness. Oh, to speak of Christ alone! This is the subject that is both “seed for the sower, and bread for the eater.” This is the live coal for the speaker’s lips, and the master key to the hearer’s heart.

modern:
Comfort yourself, tested believer, with this thought. God says, “I have chosen thee in the furnace of affliction.” Doesn’t that word come like a soft shower, cooling the fury of the flame? Yes, isn’t it fireproof armor that the heat has no power against? Let trouble come; God has chosen me. Poverty, you may march in at my door, but God is already in the house, and he has chosen me. Sickness, you may push your way in, but I have a healing balm ready: God has chosen me. Whatever happens to me in this valley of tears, I know that he has “chosen” me.

If you need still greater comfort, believer, remember *that you have the Son of Man with you in the furnace*. In that quiet room of yours, someone you haven’t seen, but whom you love, is sitting at your side. And often, when you don’t know it, he makes your bed in your illness and smooths your pillow for you. You’re poor, but the Lord of life and glory often visits that humble house of yours. He loves to come to these lonely places to visit you. Your friend stays close to you. You can’t see him, but you can feel the pressure of his hands. Don’t you hear his voice? Even in the valley of the shadow of death he says, “Fear not, I am with thee; be not dismayed, for I am thy God.” Remember Caesar’s noble words: “Fear not, thou carriest Caesar and all his fortune.” Don’t be afraid, Christian; Jesus is with you. In all your fiery trials, his presence is both your comfort and your safety. He will never leave anyone he has chosen for his own. “Fear not, for I am with thee,” is his sure promise to his chosen ones in the “furnace of affliction.” Won’t you, then, take firm hold of Christ and say,

modern: As the Spirit of God came down on the Lord Jesus, the Head, so in some measure he also comes down on the members of Christ’s spiritual body. He comes to us in the same way he came to our Lord. There’s often a remarkable *speed* about it. Before we know it, we’re carried onward and heavenward beyond anything we expected. Yet there’s none of the hurry of earthly haste, because the dove’s wings are as soft as they are swift. *Quietness* seems essential to much of the Spirit’s work. The Lord is in the still small voice, and like the dew, his grace falls in silence. The dove has always been the chosen picture of *purity*, and the Holy Spirit is holiness itself. Wherever he comes, everything pure and lovely and of good report is made to grow, and sin and uncleanness leave. *Peace* reigns too where the holy Dove comes with power. He carries the olive branch that shows the waters of God’s anger have gone down. *Gentleness* is a sure result of the holy Dove’s transforming power. Hearts touched by his kindly influence are meek and lowly from then on and forever. *Harmlessness* follows, as a matter of course. Eagles and ravens may hunt their prey, but the turtledove can bear wrong, though it can’t do wrong. We must be harmless as doves. The dove is a fitting picture of *love*: the voice of the turtledove is full of affection. And so the soul the blessed Spirit visits overflows with love to God, love to fellow believers, love to sinners, and above all love to Jesus. The brooding of the Spirit of God over the face of the deep first brought about *order and life*, and in our hearts he creates and nourishes new life and light. Blessed Spirit, as you rested on our dear Redeemer, so rest on us from now on and forever.

modern:
If none of God’s people were poor and tested, we wouldn’t know half as well the comforts of God’s grace. When we find the wanderer who has nowhere to lay his head, and yet can say, “Still will I trust in the Lord”; when we see the poor man starving on bread and water who still glories in Jesus; when we see the grieving widow overwhelmed with trouble and still trusting Christ, oh, what honor it brings the gospel! God’s grace is shown off and magnified in the poverty and trials of believers. Saints hold up under every discouragement, believing that all things work together for their good, and that real blessing will in the end spring out of what looks like evil. They believe their God will either rescue them quickly or most certainly hold them up in the trouble, for as long as he chooses to keep them in it. This patience of the saints proves the power of God’s grace.

There’s a lighthouse out at sea. On a calm night I can’t tell whether the building is solid. The storm has to rage around it, and then I’ll know whether it will stand. It’s the same with the Spirit’s work. If it weren’t often surrounded by stormy waters, we wouldn’t know it was true and strong. If the winds didn’t blow on it, we wouldn’t know how firm and secure it is. God’s masterpieces are the people who stand in the middle of difficulties, steadfast and immovable,

Anyone who wants to glorify their God must count on meeting many trials. No one can be illustrious before the Lord unless their battles are many. So if yours is a much-tested path, rejoice in it, because you’ll show all the better the all-sufficient grace of God. As for his failing you, never dream of it. Hate the thought. The God who has been enough until now should be trusted to the end.

modern:
The queen of Sheba was amazed at the richness of Solomon’s table. Her heart failed her when she saw a single day’s provisions, and she marveled just as much at the crowd of servants who were fed at the royal table. But what is this compared with the hospitality of the God of grace? Ten thousand thousand of his people are fed every day. They come to the banquet hungry and thirsty, with big appetites, but not one of them goes away unsatisfied. There’s enough for each, enough for all, enough forever. Though the crowd that feeds at the Lord’s table is as countless as the stars of heaven, each one has a share of food. Think how much grace one saint needs: so much that nothing but the Infinite could supply them for a single day. And yet the Lord spreads his table, not for one saint but for many, not for one day but for many years, and not for many years only, but for generation after generation.

Notice the full feasting the text speaks of. The guests at mercy’s banquet are satisfied, no, more than that, “abundantly satisfied,” and not with ordinary food, but with fatness, the special richness of God’s own house. And a faithful promise guarantees this feasting to all who put their trust under the shadow of the Lord’s wings. I once thought that if I could just get the leftover scraps at God’s back door of grace, I’d be satisfied, like the woman who said, “The dogs eat of the crumbs that fall from the master’s table.” But no child of God is ever served scraps and leftovers. Like Mephibosheth, they all eat from the king’s own table. In matters of grace we all get Benjamin’s portion. We all have ten times more than we could have expected, and though our needs are great, we’re often amazed at the marvelous plenty of grace God gives us to enjoy in our own experience.

modern: There are many ways of keeping Christians awake. Among them, let me strongly urge Christians to talk together about the ways of the Lord. As Christian and Hopeful journeyed toward the Celestial City, they said to themselves, “To prevent drowsiness in this place, let us fall into good discourse.” Christian asked, “Brother, where shall we begin?” And Hopeful answered, “Where God began with us.” Then Christian sang this song:

Christians who cut themselves off and walk alone are very likely to grow drowsy. Keep Christian company, and you’ll be kept awake by it, refreshed and encouraged to make quicker progress on the road to heaven. But as you take “sweet counsel” with others in the ways of God like this, make sure the subject of your conversation is the Lord Jesus. Let the eye of faith be always looking to him. Let your heart be full of him. Let your lips speak of his worth. Friend, live close to the cross, and you won’t sleep. *Work at impressing on yourself a deep sense of the value of the place you’re going to.* If you remember that you’re going to heaven, you won’t sleep on the road. If you think that hell is behind you and the devil is chasing you, you won’t dawdle. Would the man who had killed someone sleep with the avenger of blood behind him and the city of refuge ahead of him? Christian, will you sleep while the pearly gates are open, the songs of angels are waiting for you to join them and a crown of gold is ready for your head? Ah, no. In holy fellowship, keep watching and praying that you don’t enter into temptation.

modern:
What does this sweet prayer teach me? It will be my prayer this evening, but first let it give me something to think about. The text tells me, first of all, that *David had his doubts*. Why would he pray, “Say unto my soul, I am thy salvation,” if he weren’t sometimes troubled with doubts and fears? So let me take heart, because I’m not the only saint who has to complain of weak faith. If David doubted, I don’t need to conclude that I’m not a Christian because I have doubts. The text reminds me that *David wasn’t content while he had doubts and fears*. He went straight to the mercy seat to pray for assurance, because he valued it like fine gold. I too must work to have a lasting sense that I’m accepted in the Beloved, and I must take no joy when his love isn’t poured out in my soul. When my Bridegroom is gone from me, my soul must and will fast.

I also learn that *David knew where to get full assurance*. He went to his God in prayer, crying, “Say unto my soul I am thy salvation.” I must spend much time alone with God if I want a clear sense of Jesus’ love. If my prayers stop, the eye of my faith will grow dim. Much in prayer, much in heaven; slow in prayer, slow in progress. I notice that *David wouldn’t be satisfied unless his assurance came from God*. “Say unto my soul.” Lord, *you* say it! Nothing short of God’s own witness in the soul will ever satisfy the true Christian. What’s more, David couldn’t rest unless his assurance was *vividly personal*. “Say unto *my* soul, I am *thy* salvation.” Lord, if you said this to all the saints, it would mean nothing to me unless you said it to me. Lord, I have sinned. I don’t deserve your smile. I hardly dare ask for it. But oh, say to *my* soul, yes, to *my* soul, “I am *thy* salvation.” Let me have a present, personal, unmistakable, undeniable sense that I am yours and you are mine.

modern:
Regeneration is a subject that lies at the very foundation of salvation, and we should take great care to make sure we really are “born again,” because many people imagine they are who aren’t. You can be sure that the name of a Christian isn’t the nature of a Christian. Being born in a Christian country and being recognized as someone who professes the Christian religion is no use at all unless something more is added to it: being “born again.” This is so *mysterious* that human words can’t describe it. “The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof, but canst not tell whence it cometh, and whither it goeth: so is every one that is born of the Spirit.” Even so, it’s a change that is *known and felt*: known by works of holiness, and felt in a gracious experience.

This great work is *supernatural*. It isn’t something a person does for themselves. A new principle is poured in, which works in the heart, renews the soul and affects the whole person. It isn’t a change of my name, but a renewal of my nature, so that I’m not the person I used to be, but a new person in Christ Jesus. Washing and dressing a corpse is very different from bringing it to life. People can do the one; only God can do the other. So if you have been “born again,” your confession will be, “O Lord Jesus, the everlasting Father, you are my spiritual Parent. If your Spirit hadn’t breathed into me the breath of a new, holy, spiritual life, I would still be ‘dead in trespasses and sins’ today. My heavenly life comes wholly from you, and I give you all the credit for it. ‘My life is hid with Christ in God.’ It’s no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.” May the Lord help us to be fully sure on this vital point, because to be unregenerate is to be unsaved, unpardoned, without God and without hope.

modern:
There’s an old and common saying that “coming events cast their shadows before them,” and the wise man teaches us that a proud heart is the warning sign of trouble ahead. Pride is as sure a sign of destruction as the falling mercury in the barometer is of rain, and far more certain than that. When people have ridden the high horse, destruction has always caught up with them. Let David’s aching heart show how a man’s glory is eclipsed when he dotes on his own greatness ([[2Sam.24.10|2 Samuel 24:10]]). Look at Nebuchadnezzar, the mighty builder of Babylon, crawling on the ground and eating grass like an ox, until his nails grew like birds’ claws and his hair like eagles’ feathers ([[Dan.4.33|Daniel 4:33]]). Pride made the boaster a beast, as it once made an angel a devil. God hates proud looks, and he never fails to bring them down. All God’s arrows are aimed at proud hearts.

Christian, is your heart proud this evening? Pride can get into a Christian’s heart as well as a sinner’s. It can fool him into dreaming that he is “rich and increased in goods, and hath need of nothing.” Are you boasting in your graces or your talents? Are you proud of yourself because you’ve had holy moods and sweet experiences? Take note, reader: destruction is coming for you too. Your showy poppies of self-conceit will be pulled up by the roots. Your mushroom graces will wither in the burning heat. Your self-sufficiency will become like straw on the manure heap. If we forget to live at the foot of the cross in the deepest humility of spirit, God won’t forget to make us smart under his rod. Destruction will come to you, believer who thinks too highly of yourself: the destruction of your joys and comforts, though there can be no destruction of your soul. So, “He that glorieth, let him glory *in the Lord*.”

modern:
Faith is the foot of the soul, by which it marches along the road of the commandments. Love can make the feet move faster, but faith is the foot that carries the soul. Faith is the oil that lets the wheels of holy devotion and earnest godliness turn smoothly. Without faith the wheels come off the chariot, and we drag along heavily. With faith I can do all things. Without faith I’ll have neither the desire nor the power to do anything in the service of God. If you want to find the people who serve God best, look for the people with the most faith. Little faith will save someone, but little faith can’t do great things for God.

Poor Little-faith couldn’t have fought Apollyon; it took Christian to do that. Poor Little-faith couldn’t have killed Giant Despair; it took Great-heart’s arm to knock that monster down. Little faith will most certainly go to heaven, but it often has to hide itself in a nutshell, and it often loses everything but its jewels. Little-faith says, “It’s a rough road, full of sharp thorns and dangers. I’m afraid to go.” But Great-faith remembers the promise, “Thy shoes shall be iron and brass; as thy days, so shall thy strength be,” and so she boldly sets out. Little-faith stands discouraged, adding her tears to the flood. But Great-faith sings, “When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee,” and she wades across the stream at once.

Do you want to be comfortable and happy? Do you want to enjoy your faith? Do you want a cheerful religion and not a gloomy one? Then “have faith in God.” If you love darkness and are content to live in gloom and misery, then be satisfied with little faith. But if you love the sunshine and want to sing songs of joy, earnestly desire this best gift, “great faith.”

notes.note: Devotion to God; faith as it’s actually lived.
In John Bunyan’s *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, a weak pilgrim who is robbed on the road but keeps his jewels, his assurance of heaven, and gets there in the end.
The demon Christian fights in the Valley of Humiliation in *The Pilgrim’s Progress*. The name, “Destroyer,” comes from [[Rev.9.11|Revelation 9:11]].
From the second part of *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, where the brave guide Great-heart kills the giant who had imprisoned Christian in Doubting Castle.

notes.term: “Thy shoes shall be iron and brass…”
notes.note: Moses’ blessing on Asher ([[Deut.33.25|Deuteronomy 33:25]]).
Discouraged, losing heart.
Desire eagerly. “Covet earnestly the best gifts” ([[1Cor.12.31|1 Corinthians 12:31]]).

modern:
No doubt you’ve been tempted, reader, to rely on the things you can see, instead of resting only on the invisible God. Christians often look to people for help and advice, and spoil the noble simplicity of their trust in their God. If this evening’s reading meets the eye of a child of God anxious about the things of this life, then we’d like to reason with you for a while. You trust in Jesus, and only Jesus, for your salvation, so why are you troubled? “*Because of my great worries.*” Isn’t it written, “Cast thy burden upon the Lord”? “Be careful for nothing, but in everything by prayer and supplication make known your wants unto God.” Can’t you trust God for the things of this life? “*Ah, I wish I could!*” If you can’t trust God for earthly things, how dare you trust him for spiritual things? Can you trust him to redeem your soul and not rely on him for a few lesser mercies? Isn’t God enough for your need? Is his all-sufficiency too small for your wants? Do you need another eye besides his, who sees every secret thing? Is his heart faint? Is his arm tired? If so, look for another God. But if he is infinite, almighty, faithful, true and all-wise, why do you go wandering around so much looking for something else to trust? Why rake through the earth for another foundation, when this one is strong enough to bear all the weight you could ever build on it?

Christian, don’t water down your wine. Don’t mix the gold of faith with the dross of trusting people. Wait only on God, and let your expectation be from him. Don’t long for Jonah’s gourd, but rest in Jonah’s God. Let fools choose the sandy foundations of earthly trust, but you, like someone who sees the storm coming, build yourself a lasting home on the Rock of Ages.

notes.note: The things of this life: money, food, health and so on.
Spoil.
Worry, anxiety.
From [[Phil.4.6|Philippians 4:6]]. “Careful” means anxious.
Do you go wandering about? “Why gaddest thou about so much?” ([[Jer.2.36|Jeremiah 2:36]]).
A cheaper metal mixed into gold, and the scum of impurities skimmed off it.

notes.term: Let thine expectation be from him
notes.note: “My soul, wait thou only upon God; for my expectation is from him” ([[Ps.62.5|Psalm 62:5]]).
The plant that shaded Jonah and then withered overnight ([[Jonah.4.6-Jonah.4.7|Jonah 4:6–7]]).
A name for God, from the margin of [[Isa.26.4|Isaiah 26:4]], made famous by Toplady’s hymn.

modern:
God’s people have their trials. When God chose his people, he never meant them to be untested. They were chosen in the furnace of affliction, never chosen for worldly peace and earthly joy. Freedom from sickness and the pains of mortal life was never promised them. When their Lord drew up the charter of their privileges, he included discipline among the things they would certainly inherit. Trials are part of our lot. They were planned for us beforehand in Christ’s last will and testament. As surely as the stars are shaped by his hands and their orbits fixed by him, so surely are our trials assigned to us. He has appointed their time and place, their strength and the effect they will have on us. Good people must never expect to escape trouble. If they do, they’ll be disappointed, because none who went before them were without it. Notice the patience of Job. Remember Abraham: he had his trials, and through his faith in them he became the “Father of the faithful.” Look carefully at the life stories of all the patriarchs, prophets, apostles and martyrs, and you won’t find one of those God made vessels of mercy who wasn’t made to pass through the fire of affliction.

It was settled long ago that the cross of trouble would be engraved on every vessel of mercy, as the royal mark that sets apart the King’s vessels of honor. But though trouble is the path of God’s children, they have the comfort of knowing that their Master walked it before them. They have his presence and sympathy to cheer them, his grace to hold them up and his example to teach them how to endure. And when they reach “the kingdom,” it will more than make up for the “much tribulation” they went through to get there.

notes.note: Trouble, suffering.
Trouble pictured as a refiner’s furnace ([[Isa.48.10|Isaiah 48:10]]).
Discipline, correction.
Planned and decided beforehand by God.
Jesus’ parting words: “In the world ye shall have tribulation: but be of good cheer; I have overcome the world” ([[John.16.33|John 16:33]]).
“Ye have heard of the patience of Job” ([[Jas.5.11|James 5:11]]).
A traditional title for Abraham, “the father of all them that believe” ([[Rom.4.11|Romans 4:11]]).
People God has shaped to receive his mercy ([[Rom.9.23|Romans 9:23]]).
Make up for something.

modern:
Every situation has a bright side as well as a dark one. Rachel was overwhelmed with the sorrow of her own labor and death. Jacob, though weeping for the mother he had lost, could see the mercy of the child’s birth. It’s good for us if, while the flesh mourns over trials, our faith triumphs in God’s faithfulness. Samson’s lion gave honey, and so will our troubles, if we look at them rightly. The stormy sea feeds multitudes with its fish. The wild woods bloom with lovely flowers. The stormy wind sweeps away disease, and the biting frost loosens the soil. Dark clouds drop bright drops, and black earth grows bright flowers. There’s a vein of good to be found in every mine of evil.

Sad hearts have a special talent for finding the worst angle to look at a trial from. If there were only one bog in the world, they’d soon be up to their necks in it, and if there were only one lion in the desert, they’d hear it roar. There’s a touch of this miserable foolishness in all of us, and at times, like Jacob, we’re quick to cry, “All these things are against me.” Faith’s way of walking is to throw all her worries on the Lord, and then to expect good results from the worst disasters. Like Gideon’s men, she doesn’t fret over the broken pitcher, but rejoices that the lamp blazes out all the more. Out of the rough oyster shell of difficulty she draws the rare pearl of honor, and from the deep ocean caves of distress she brings up the priceless coral of experience. When her tide of prosperity goes out, she finds treasures hidden in the sand. When her sun of delight goes down, she turns her telescope of hope to the starry promises of heaven. When death itself appears, faith points to the light of resurrection beyond the grave, and so turns our dying Benoni into our living Benjamin.

notes.note: Rachel died giving birth and named her son “son of my sorrow,” but Jacob renamed him “son of my right hand” ([[Gen.35.18|Genesis 35:18]]).
Labor in childbirth.
Samson killed a lion, and later found bees and honey in its carcass ([[Judg.14.8|Judges 14:8]]).
A deadly epidemic.
A bog or swamp. In *The Pilgrim’s Progress*, the Slough of Despond is the bog of despair.
Jacob’s cry when he thought he had lost Joseph and would lose Benjamin too ([[Gen.42.36|Genesis 42:36]]). In fact, all those things were working for his good.
Gideon’s three hundred carried lamps hidden in clay pitchers, and smashed the pitchers so the lights blazed out ([[Judg.7.20|Judges 7:20]]).
Goes out, as the tide does.

modern:
The supreme beauty of Jesus draws everything to itself. It isn’t so much something to admire as something to love. He is more than pleasant and fair; he is lovely. Surely God’s people can fully justify using this golden word, because he is the object of their warmest love, a love based on the true excellence of his person, the complete perfection of his charms. Look at your Master’s lips, disciples of Jesus, and say, “Aren’t they most sweet?” Don’t his words make your hearts burn within you as he talks with you on the road? You who worship Immanuel, look up at his head of finest gold, and tell me: aren’t his thoughts precious to you? Isn’t your worship sweetened with affection as you humbly bow before that face, which is like Lebanon, excellent as the cedars? Isn’t there a charm in every feature? Isn’t his whole person so fragrant with the scent of his good perfumes that the young women love him? Is there one part of his glorious body that isn’t attractive, one part of his person that isn’t a fresh magnet to our souls, one of his offices that isn’t a strong cord binding your heart?

Our love isn’t set like a seal on his loving heart alone; it’s fastened on his arm of power too. There isn’t a single part of him our love doesn’t fasten on. We anoint his whole person with the sweet perfume of our burning love. We want to copy his whole life and write out his whole character in ours. In every other being we see something lacking; in him there’s complete perfection. Even the best of his favored saints have had stains on their clothes and wrinkles on their foreheads. He is nothing but loveliness. Every earthly sun has its spots. The lovely world itself has its wilderness. We can’t love every part of the loveliest thing. But Christ Jesus is gold without alloy, light without darkness, glory without a cloud. “Yea, he is *altogether* lovely.”

notes.note: The bride’s description of her beloved ([[Song.5.16|Song of Solomon 5:16]]).
Belonging to its very nature.
“His mouth is most sweet” ([[Song.5.16|Song of Solomon 5:16]]).
Like the two on the road to Emmaus: “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?” ([[Luke.24.32|Luke 24:32]]).

notes.term: His head of much fine gold
notes.note: “His head is as the most fine gold… his countenance is as Lebanon, excellent as the cedars” ([[Song.5.11|Song of Solomon 5:11]]; [[Song.5.15|5:15]]).
“Because of the savour of thy good ointments… therefore do the virgins love thee” ([[Song.1.3|Song of Solomon 1:3]]).
A naturally magnetic stone.

notes.term: As a seal… upon his arm
notes.note: “Set me as a seal upon thine heart, as a seal upon thine arm” ([[Song.8.6|Song of Solomon 8:6]]).
A costly perfumed oil ([[Song.1.12|Song of Solomon 1:12]]).
A cheaper metal mixed into a precious one.

modern:
Fellowship with Christ is a sure cure for every ill. Whether it’s the bitter wormwood of sorrow or the sickening excess of earthly pleasure, close fellowship with the Lord Jesus will take the bitterness out of the one and the overfullness out of the other. Live close to Jesus, Christian, and it matters very little whether you live on the mountain of honor or in the valley of humiliation. Living close to Jesus, you’re covered by God’s wings, and the everlasting arms are underneath you. Don’t let anything keep you from that holy fellowship, the choicest privilege of a soul married to the Well-beloved. Don’t be content with a meeting now and then, but always try to keep his company, because only in his presence do you have comfort or safety. Jesus shouldn’t be a friend who drops in on us now and then, but one we walk with all the time.

You have a hard road ahead of you. Traveler to heaven, make sure you don’t set out without your guide. You have to go through the fiery furnace. Don’t go in unless, like Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, you have the Son of God as your companion. You have to storm the Jericho of your own sinful desires. Don’t start the war until, like Joshua, you’ve seen the Captain of the Lord’s army with his sword drawn in his hand. You have to meet the Esau of your many temptations. Don’t meet him until, at the brook Jabbok, you’ve taken hold of the angel and won. In every situation, in every state, you’ll need Jesus, but most of all when the iron gates of death open for you. Stay close to your soul’s Husband. Lean your head on his chest. Ask to be refreshed with the spiced wine of his pomegranates, and he will find you at the end without spot or wrinkle or any such thing. Since you’ve lived with him and lived in him here, you’ll stay with him forever.

notes.note: Remain, stay, live in.
A bitter plant; a picture of bitter sorrow.
Sickening overindulgence, like eating too many sweets.
Being overfull; having had too much.
“The eternal God is thy refuge, and underneath are the everlasting arms” ([[Deut.33.27|Deuteronomy 33:27]]).
In older English, conversation and fellowship.
Daniel’s three friends, thrown into the fiery furnace, where a fourth figure “like the Son of God” walked with them ([[Dan.3.25|Daniel 3:25]]).

notes.term: The Captain of the Lord’s host
notes.note: The commander of the Lord’s army, who met Joshua before Jericho with a drawn sword ([[Josh.5.13-Josh.5.14|Joshua 5:13–14]]).
Where Jacob wrestled all night with the angel before meeting his brother Esau, and would not let go until he was blessed ([[Gen.32.22-Gen.32.28|Genesis 32:22–28]]).
“I would cause thee to drink of spiced wine of the juice of my pomegranate” ([[Song.8.2|Song of Solomon 8:2]]).
Christ’s church presented as a radiant bride ([[Eph.5.27|Ephesians 5:27]]).

modern:
“Moab settled on his lees, he hath not been emptied from vessel to vessel.” Give someone wealth. Let his ships keep bringing home rich cargoes. Let the winds and waves seem to be his servants, carrying his ships across the wide sea. Let his lands produce plenty. Let the weather favor his crops. Let unbroken success follow him. Let him stand among people as a successful merchant. Let him enjoy constant health. Let him march through the world with steady nerves and bright eyes, and live happily. Give him high spirits. Let a song always be on his lips. Let his eyes always sparkle with joy. The natural result of such an easy life, for anyone, even if he were the best Christian who ever lived, will be *presumption*. Even David said, “I shall never be moved,” and we’re no better than David, or even half as good.

My friend, beware of the smooth places on the road. If you’re walking on them, or if the road is rough, thank God for it. If God always rocked us in the cradle of prosperity; if we were always bounced on the knees of fortune; if there were no stain on the alabaster pillar, no clouds in the sky, no bitter drops in the wine of this life, we would get drunk with pleasure. We’d dream “we stand,” and stand we would, but on a pinnacle, like the man asleep on top of the mast, in danger every moment.

So we bless God for our troubles. We thank him for our changes. We praise his name for our losses of property, because we feel that if he hadn’t disciplined us like this, we might have become too secure. Constant worldly prosperity is a fiery trial.

notes.note: From [[Jer.48.11|Jeremiah 48:11]]. Wine left to sit on its dregs (lees) without being poured from jar to jar grows thick and stale; Moab’s easy life had left it unchanged and complacent.
Favorable.
Cheerful, light-hearted.
Taking things for granted; overconfidence.
David’s words in [[Ps.30.6|Psalm 30:6]], just before he admits, “thou didst hide thy face, and I was troubled.”
Bounced on someone’s knee, like a baby.
“Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” ([[1Cor.10.12|1 Corinthians 10:12]]).

notes.term: The man asleep upon the mast
notes.note: “As he that lieth upon the top of a mast” ([[Prov.23.34|Proverbs 23:34]]): a picture of someone carelessly at ease in great danger.
Disciplined, corrected.

modern:
It may do us great good, before we fall asleep, to remember this sad fact, because it may lead us to hold earthly things loosely. There’s nothing very pleasant in remembering that we aren’t out of reach of the arrows of trouble, but it may humble us and keep us from boasting like the psalmist in our morning reading: “My mountain standeth firm: I shall never be moved.” It may stop us putting down roots too deep in this soil, when we’re so soon to be transplanted into the heavenly garden.

Let’s remember how loosely we hold our *earthly mercies*. If we remembered that all the trees of earth are marked for the woodcutter’s axe, we wouldn’t be so quick to build our nests in them. We should love, but we should love with a love that expects death and reckons on partings. Our dear relatives are only lent to us, and the hour when we must hand them back to the Lender may be right at the door. The same is certainly true of our *worldly goods*. Don’t riches sprout wings and fly away? Our *health* is just as uncertain. We’re frail flowers of the field, and we mustn’t count on blooming forever. There’s a time appointed for weakness and sickness, when we’ll have to glorify God by suffering rather than by busy activity. There’s no single point where we can hope to escape the sharp arrows of affliction. Out of our few days, not one is safe from sorrow. A person’s life is a barrel full of bitter wine; whoever looks for joy in it might as well look for honey in an ocean of salt water.

Dear reader, don’t set your heart on the things of earth. Seek the things above, because *here* the moth eats and the thief breaks in, but *there* all joys are lasting and eternal. The path of trouble is the way home. Lord, make this thought a pillow for many a weary head!

notes.term: Of few days, and full of trouble
notes.note: Job’s words about every human life ([[Job.14.1|Job 14:1]]).
Hold loosely; care less for.
Spurgeon blends [[Ps.30.6-Ps.30.7|Psalm 30:6–7]]: “I shall never be moved. LORD, by thy favour thou hast made my mountain to stand strong.”
The terms on which something is held, as a tenant holds a house.
Good things for this life only.
“Riches certainly make themselves wings; they fly away as an eagle toward heaven” ([[Prov.23.5|Proverbs 23:5]]).
Uncertain, easily lost.
Salt water.

notes.term: Seek those things which are above
notes.note: [[Col.3.1-Col.3.2|Colossians 3:1–2]].
“Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt, and where thieves break through and steal” ([[Matt.6.19-Matt.6.20|Matthew 6:19–20]]).

modern:
Beware of taking sin lightly. When we’re first converted, our conscience is so tender that we’re afraid of the slightest sin. New converts have a holy shyness, a godly fear of offending God. But sadly, the fine bloom on these first ripe fruits is soon rubbed off by the rough handling of the world around them. The sensitive plant of young godliness turns into a willow later in life, too bendy, too easily giving way. It’s sadly true that even a Christian can gradually grow so hardened that the sin that once startled him doesn’t alarm him at all. Little by little people get used to sin. An ear that has heard cannon booming won’t notice small sounds. At first a little sin startles us, but soon we say, “Is it not a little one?” Then comes another, bigger one, and then another, until little by little we come to think of sin as only a small evil. And then comes an unholy presumption: “We haven’t fallen into open sin. True, we tripped a little, but on the whole we stayed upright. We may have said one unholy word, but most of our conversation has been consistent.” So we excuse sin. We throw a cloak over it. We call it by pretty names.

Christian, beware of thinking lightly of sin. Be careful you don’t fall little by little. Sin, a *little* thing? Isn’t it a poison? Who knows how deadly it is? Sin, a little thing? Don’t the little foxes spoil the vines? Doesn’t the tiny coral creature build a reef that wrecks a fleet? Don’t little strokes fell tall oaks? Won’t constant dripping wear away stones? Sin, a little thing? It put thorns around the Redeemer’s head and pierced his heart! It made him suffer anguish, bitterness and woe. If you could weigh the smallest sin on the scales of eternity, you’d run from it as from a snake, and hate even the appearance of evil. Look on all sin as what crucified the Savior, and you’ll see it to be “exceeding sinful.”

notes.note: Paul says the law shows sin up for what it is: “that sin by the commandment might become exceeding sinful” ([[Rom.7.13|Romans 7:13]]).
Devotion to God; faith as it’s actually lived.
Hardened, unfeeling.
Lot’s plea to be allowed to flee to the small town of Zoar ([[Gen.19.20|Genesis 19:20]]). Spurgeon turns it into the excuse we make for a “small” sin.
Taking things for granted; overconfidence.
Excuse; make something seem less serious.
“The little foxes, that spoil the vines” ([[Song.2.15|Song of Solomon 2:15]]).

notes.term: Abhor the least appearance of evil
notes.note: “Abstain from all appearance of evil” ([[1Thess.5.22|1 Thessalonians 5:22]]).

modern: God’s overwhelming grace shows very clearly in this: we weren’t only sought, but sought *out*. People *look* for something that’s lost on the floor of the house, but that’s only looking, not seeking out. When something is sought *out*, the loss is more baffling and the search more persistent. We were mixed in with the mud. We were like a precious piece of gold that has fallen into the sewer, so that people have to dig out and carefully examine a mass of disgusting filth, and keep on stirring and raking and searching through the heap until the treasure is found. Or, to use another picture, we were lost in a maze. We wandered here and there, and when mercy came after us with the gospel, it didn’t find us the first time. It had to search for us and seek us out. We were lost sheep, so desperately lost, wandered into such strange country, that it didn’t seem possible even the Good Shepherd could track our winding ramblings. Glory to unconquerable grace, we were sought *out*! No darkness could hide us, no filth could conceal us. We were found and brought home. Glory to infinite love, God the Holy Spirit brought us back!

The lives of some of God’s people, if they could be written, would fill us with holy amazement. Strange and marvelous are the ways God used to find his own in their case. Blessed be his name, he never gives up the search until his chosen ones have been effectively sought out. They aren’t a people sought today and thrown away tomorrow. Almighty power and wisdom together make no failures. They will be called “*Sought out*!” That anyone should be sought out is matchless grace, but that *we* should be sought out is grace beyond measure! We can find no reason for it but God’s own sovereign love, and we can only lift up our hearts in wonder and praise the Lord that tonight we wear the name “*Sought out*.”

notes.note: A new name God gives Jerusalem: “thou shalt be called, Sought out, A city not forsaken” ([[Isa.62.12|Isaiah 62:12]]).
A maze.
Here and there.
Jesus, who goes after the lost sheep “until he find it” ([[Luke.15.4|Luke 15:4]]).
Winding, wandering paths.
Gives up.
Love freely chosen by God, not earned by us.

modern: “Love thy neighbour.” Maybe he’s rolling in riches and you’re poor, living in your little cottage right next to his grand mansion. Every day you see his estates, his fine clothes and his lavish dinners. God has given him these gifts. Don’t covet his wealth, and don’t think hard thoughts about him. Be content with your own lot, if you can’t improve it, but don’t look at your neighbor and wish he were in your position. Love him, and then you won’t envy him.

Or maybe it’s the other way around: you’re rich, and poor people live near you. Don’t scorn to call them neighbor. Admit that you’re bound to love them. The world calls them your inferiors. In what way are they inferior? They’re far more your equals than your inferiors, because “God hath made of one blood all people that dwell upon the face of the earth.” It’s your coat that’s better than theirs, but you’re not one bit better than they are. They’re human beings, and what more are you than that? Make sure you love your neighbor, even if he’s in rags or sunk in the depths of poverty.

But maybe you say, “I can’t love my neighbors, because whatever I do, they repay me with ingratitude and contempt.” Then there’s all the more room for the heroism of love. Would you rather be a feather-bed soldier than fight love’s rough battle? Whoever dares most will win most. If your path of love is rough, walk it boldly, and keep on loving your neighbors through thick and thin. Heap coals of fire on their heads. And if they’re hard to please, don’t try to please *them*, but to please *your Master*. Remember that if *they* reject your love, your Master hasn’t rejected it, and your deed is as welcome to him as if it had been welcome to them. Love your neighbor, because in doing so you’re following in the footsteps of Christ.

notes.note: The great command, which Jesus quotes in [[Matt.5.43-Matt.5.44|Matthew 5:43–44]], adding that we must love our enemies too.
A cottage.
Lavish, expensive.
Want what belongs to someone else.
From Paul’s words in Athens, [[Acts.17.26|Acts 17:26]], “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth.”
A soldier who only fights from the comfort of his bed.

notes.term: Heap coals of fire on their heads
notes.note: Shame enemies into regret by being kind to them ([[Rom.12.20|Romans 12:20]]).

modern: There’s no neutral ground in religion. Either we’re enlisted under the banner of Prince Immanuel, to serve and fight his battles, or we’re subjects of the black prince, Satan. “To whom belongest thou?”

Reader, let me help you with your answer. *Have you been “born again”?* If you have, you belong to Christ, but without the new birth you can’t be his. *Who do you trust?* Because those who believe in Jesus are the children of God. *Whose work are you doing?* You’re sure to serve your master, because whoever you serve is thereby owned as your lord. *What company do you keep?* If you belong to Jesus, you’ll make friends with those who wear the uniform of the cross. “Birds of a feather flock together.” *What is your conversation like?* Is it heavenly or earthly? *What have you learned from your Master?* Servants learn a great deal from the masters they’re apprenticed to. If you’ve served your time with Jesus, it will be said of you, as it was of Peter and John, “They took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”

We press the question: “To whom belongest thou?” Answer honestly before you close your eyes in sleep. If you aren’t Christ’s, you’re in a hard service. *Run away from your cruel master!* Enter the service of the Lord of Love, and you’ll enjoy a blessed life. If you *are* Christ’s, let me advise you to do four things. You belong to Jesus, so *obey him*. Let his word be your law; let his wish be your will. You belong to the Beloved, so *love him*. Let your heart embrace him; let your whole soul be filled with him. You belong to the Son of God, so *trust him*. Rest nowhere but on him. You belong to the King of kings, so *be decided for him*. Then, without any brand on your forehead, everyone will know who you belong to.

notes.note: David’s question to an abandoned Egyptian slave he found in a field ([[1Sam.30.13|1 Samuel 30:13]]).
A name for Christ from John Bunyan’s allegory *The Holy War*, in which he wins back the town of Mansoul.
Servants bound to a lord.
Make friends, keep company.
The uniform worn by the servants of a great household.
In older English, your whole way of life, not only your talk.
Slaves were sometimes branded with their owner’s mark. God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads in John’s vision ([[Rev.7.3|Revelation 7:3]]).

modern:
Dear reader, this little book was written mainly to build up believers, but if you aren’t saved yet, our heart longs over you, and we would love to say a word that God might bless to you. Open your Bible and read the story of the lepers, and notice their position, which was very much like yours. If you stay where you are, you must perish. If you go to Jesus, the worst that can happen is that you die. “Nothing venture, nothing win,” says the old proverb, and in your case the risk isn’t a great one. If you sit still in sullen despair, no one can pity you when your ruin comes. But if you died having sought mercy, if such a thing were possible, everyone would feel for you. No one who refuses to look to Jesus escapes. But you know that, at any rate, some who believe in him are saved, because some of the people you know have received mercy. So why not you? The people of Nineveh said, “Who can tell?” Act on the same hope, and try the Lord’s mercy. Perishing is so dreadful that if there were only a straw to grab at, the instinct to save yourself should make you reach out your hand.

So far we’ve been talking to you on your own unbelieving ground. Now we want to assure you, as from the Lord, that if you seek him, you will find him. Jesus throws out no one who comes to him. You won’t perish if you trust him. On the contrary, you’ll find treasure far richer than the poor lepers gathered in the abandoned Syrian camp. May the Holy Spirit give you courage to go at once, and you won’t believe in vain. When you’re saved yourself, spread the good news to others. Don’t keep quiet. Tell the King’s household first, and join them in fellowship. Let the city gatekeeper, the minister, know about your discovery, and then announce the good news everywhere. May the Lord save you before the sun goes down today.

modern:
Worn out with her wanderings, the dove comes back at last to the ark, her only resting place. How heavily she flies! She’ll drop; she’ll never reach the ark! But she struggles on. Noah has been watching for his dove all day long, and he’s ready to take her in. She has just enough strength to reach the edge of the ark. She can hardly land on it and is about to fall, when Noah puts out his hand and pulls her in to himself. Notice that: “*pulled her in unto him*.” She didn’t fly right in by herself. She was too frightened or too tired to do it. She flew as far as she could, and then he put out his hand and pulled her in to himself. This kindness was shown to the wandering dove, and she wasn’t scolded for wandering. Just as she was, she was pulled into the ark.

In the same way, seeking sinner, you’ll be received with all your sin. “Only return”: those are God’s two gracious words. “Only return.” What? Nothing else? No, “only return.” She had no olive branch in her beak this time, nothing at all but herself and her wanderings. But it’s “only return,” and she does return, and Noah pulls her in. Fly, wanderer; fly, fainting one, dove that you are, even if you think yourself as black as the raven with the mud of sin. Back, back to the Savior! Every moment you wait only adds to your misery. Your attempts to preen yourself and make yourself fit for Jesus are all useless. Come to him just as you are. “Return, thou backsliding Israel.” He doesn’t say, “Return, thou *repenting* Israel” (there is an invitation like that, no doubt), but “thou *backsliding* one,” a backslider with all your backslidings on you. Return, return, return! Jesus is waiting for you! He’ll stretch out his hand and “pull you in,” in to himself, your heart’s true home.

notes.note: Noah sent out a dove from the ark; finding nowhere to land, she came back and Noah took her in ([[Gen.8.8-Gen.8.9|Genesis 8:8–9]]).

modern:
It’s a curious fact that people can be proud of grace. One says, “I have great faith. I won’t fall. Poor little faith may, but I never will.” “I have burning love,” says another. “I can stand. There’s no danger of my going astray.” Whoever boasts of grace has little grace to boast of. Some who do this imagine their graces can keep them going, not knowing that the stream must keep flowing from the spring or the brook will soon run dry. If oil doesn’t keep flowing to the lamp, it may burn brightly today, but tomorrow it will smoke, and the smell will be foul. Take care not to boast in your graces. Let all your boasting and confidence be in Christ and his strength, because that’s the only way you can be kept from falling.

Pray much more. Spend longer in holy worship. Read the Scriptures more earnestly and constantly. Watch your life more carefully. Live closer to God. Take the best examples as your pattern. Let your conversation be fragrant with heaven. Let your hearts be perfumed with love for people’s souls. Live so that people can see you’ve been with Jesus and learned from him. And when that happy day comes, when the One you love says, “Come up higher,” may you have the joy of hearing him say, “Thou hast fought a good fight, thou hast finished thy course, and henceforth there is laid up for thee a crown of righteousness which fadeth not away.” On, Christian, with care and caution! On, with holy fear and trembling! On, with faith and confidence in Jesus alone, and let your constant prayer be, “Uphold me according to thy word.” He is able, and he alone, “To keep you from falling, and to present you faultless before the presence of his glory with exceeding joy.”

notes.note: Harmful, foul.

modern:
Fellow pilgrim, don’t say in your heart, “I’ll go here and there, and I won’t sin.” You’re never so far out of danger of sinning that you can boast of being safe. The road is very muddy; it will be hard to pick your way without dirtying your clothes. This is a world of tar. You’ll need to keep watch often if you’re going to handle it and keep your hands clean. There’s a robber at every bend in the road waiting to steal your jewels. There’s a temptation in every mercy. There’s a trap in every joy. If you ever reach heaven, it will be a miracle of God’s grace, to be credited entirely to your Father’s power.

Be on your guard. When someone carries a bombshell in his hand, he should be careful not to go near a candle, and you too must take care not to walk into temptation. Even your ordinary actions are sharp tools; you have to be careful how you handle them. There’s nothing in this world to nourish a Christian’s godliness, but everything to destroy it. How eager you should be to look up to God, so that *he* will keep you! Your prayer should be, “Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe.” And having prayed, you must also watch, guarding every thought, word and action with holy jealousy. Don’t expose yourself to danger needlessly. But if you’re called to it, if you’re sent where the arrows are flying, never go out without your shield. Because once the devil finds you without your shield, he’ll be glad his hour of triumph has come, and he’ll soon have you down, wounded by his arrows. You can’t be killed, but you may be wounded. “Be sober; be vigilant, danger may be in an hour when all seemeth securest to thee.” So take heed to your ways, and watch and pray. No one ever went wrong by being too watchful. May the Holy Spirit guide us in all our ways, and then they’ll always please the Lord.

notes.note: David’s resolve “that I sin not with my tongue” ([[Ps.39.1|Psalm 39:1]]).

modern:
Christ has grace without limit in himself, but he hasn’t kept it for himself. As a reservoir empties itself into the pipes, so Christ has emptied out his grace for his people. “Of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.” He seems to have it only so that he can hand it out to us. He stands like a fountain, always flowing, but flowing only to fill the empty pitchers and thirsty lips that come near it. Like a tree, he bears sweet fruit, not to hang on the branches, but to be picked by those who need it. Grace, whether its work is to pardon, to cleanse, to keep, to strengthen, to enlighten, to give life or to restore, can always be had from him freely and without price, and there’s no form of the work of grace he hasn’t given to his people. As the blood of the body flows from the heart but belongs equally to every part, so the workings of grace are the inheritance of every saint joined to the Lamb.

And here there’s a sweet fellowship between Christ and his church, because they both receive the same grace. Christ is the head the oil is first poured on, but the same oil runs down to the very hem of the clothes, so that the humblest saint has an anointing of the same costly oil that fell on the head. This is true fellowship: when the sap of grace flows from the trunk to the branch, and we see that the trunk itself is kept alive by the very nourishment that feeds the branch. As we receive grace from Jesus day by day, and more and more recognize that it comes from him, we’ll see him in fellowship with us and enjoy the happiness of fellowship with him. Let’s use our riches every day, and always go to him as our own Lord by covenant, taking from him the supply of everything we need as boldly as people take money from their own purse.

notes.note: “God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto him” ([[John.3.34|John 3:34]]).

modern:
This is nothing unusual. It’s the general rule of the moral universe that people who do their work with all their hearts prosper, while those who go to work leaving half their hearts behind are almost sure to fail. God doesn’t give harvests to lazy people, except harvests of thistles, and he isn’t pleased to send wealth to people who won’t dig in the field to find its hidden treasure. Everyone agrees that if someone wants to prosper, they must work hard at their business. It’s the same in religion as in other things. If you want to prosper in your work for Jesus, let it be *heart* work, and let it be done with *all* your heart. Put as much force, energy, heartiness and earnestness into your faith as you ever put into your business, because it deserves far more. The Holy Spirit helps our weaknesses, but he doesn’t encourage our laziness. He loves active believers.

Who are the most useful people in the Christian church? The ones who do what they take on for God *with all their hearts*. Who are the most successful Sunday school teachers? The most talented? No: the most zealous, the ones whose hearts are on fire. Those are the people who see their Lord riding out victoriously in the majesty of his salvation. Wholeheartedness shows itself in *perseverance*. There may be failure at first, but the earnest worker will say, “It’s the Lord’s work, and it must be done. My Lord has told me to do it, and in his strength I’ll get it done.” Christian, are you serving your Master like this, “with all thine heart”? Remember how earnest Jesus was! Think what heart work his was! He could say, “*The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up*.” When he sweat great drops of blood, it was no light burden he carried on those blessed shoulders. And when he poured out his heart, it was no feeble effort he was making for the salvation of his people. Was Jesus in earnest, and are we lukewarm?

modern:
Yes, O Lord, a stranger *with* you, but not *to* you. Your grace has effectively removed all my natural distance from you, and now, in fellowship with you, I walk through this sinful world like a pilgrim in a foreign country. *You* are a stranger in your own world. People forget you, dishonor you, set up new laws and foreign customs, and don’t know you. When your dear Son came to his own, his own didn’t receive him. He was in the world, and the world was made by him, and the world didn’t know him. No foreigner was ever so much the odd one out among the people of any country as your beloved Son was among his mother’s people. So it’s no wonder if I, who live the life of Jesus, am unknown and a stranger here below. Lord, I don’t want to be a citizen where Jesus was a foreigner. His pierced hand has loosened the cords that once tied my soul to earth, and now I find myself a stranger in the land. My speech sounds like a foreign language to these Babylonians I live among. My manners are odd, and my actions strange. A Tartar would be more at home in a London shopping street than I could ever be in the haunts of sinners.

But here is the sweetness of my lot: I’m a stranger *with you*. You’re my fellow sufferer, my fellow pilgrim. Oh, what joy to wander in such blessed company! My heart burns within me on the road when you speak to me, and though I’m only passing through, I’m far more blessed than those who sit on thrones, and far more at home than those who live in their paneled houses.

notes.note: From David’s prayer: “I am a stranger with thee, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were” ([[Ps.39.12|Psalm 39:12]]).

modern:
This was the *prayer of the “man after God’s own heart.”* Did holy David need to pray like this? Then how much must we babies in grace need such a prayer! It’s as if he said, “Hold me back, or I’ll rush headlong over the cliff of sin.” Our evil nature, like a bad-tempered horse, is quick to bolt. May the grace of God put a bridle on it and hold it in, so it doesn’t rush into trouble. What might even the best of us do if it weren’t for the checks the Lord puts on us, in his providence and in his grace!

The psalmist’s prayer is aimed at the worst kind of sin: sin committed deliberately and willfully. Even the holiest need to be “kept back” from the vilest wrongs. It’s a solemn thing to find the apostle Paul warning saints against the most disgusting sins: “Mortify therefore your members which are upon the earth; fornication, uncleanness, inordinate affection, evil concupiscence, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” What! Do saints need warning against sins like these? Yes, they do. The whitest robes, unless God’s grace keeps them pure, will be stained with the blackest spots. Experienced Christian, don’t boast of your experience. You’ll trip yet if you look away from the One who is able to keep you from falling. You whose love is burning, whose faith is steady, whose hopes are bright, don’t say, “We’ll never sin,” but cry instead, “Lead us not into temptation.” There’s enough tinder in the heart of the best person to light a fire that would burn to the lowest hell, unless God puts out the sparks as they fall. Who would have dreamed that righteous Lot could be found drunk and committing uncleanness? Hazael said, “Is thy servant a dog, that he should do this thing?” and we’re very quick to ask the same self-righteous question. May infinite wisdom cure us of the madness of self-confidence.

modern:
Why does God let so many of his children be poor? He could make them all rich if he wanted to. He could lay bags of gold at their doors. He could send them a large yearly income. Or he could scatter plenty of food around their houses, as he once made the quail lie in heaps around Israel’s camp and rained bread from heaven to feed them. There’s no need for them to be poor, except that he sees it’s best. “The cattle upon a thousand hills are his.” He could supply them. He could make the richest, greatest and mightiest bring all their power and riches to his children’s feet, because every human heart is under his control. But he doesn’t choose to. He lets them go without; he lets them waste away in poverty and obscurity.

Why is this? There are many reasons. One is *to give those of us who have been blessed with enough a chance to show our love to Jesus*. We show our love to Christ when we sing about him and pray to him. But if there were no needy people in the world, we’d lose the sweet privilege of proving our love by giving to his poorer brothers and sisters. He has arranged things so that in this way we can prove our love isn’t only in word, but in deed and in truth. If we really love Christ, we’ll care for those he loves. Those who are dear to him will be dear to us. So let’s see helping the poor of the Lord’s flock not as a duty but as a privilege, remembering the words of the Lord Jesus: “Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.” Surely this assurance is sweet enough, and this reason strong enough, to make us help others with a willing hand and a loving heart, remembering that Christ graciously accepts everything we do for his people as done for himself.

notes.note: The one thing the apostles in Jerusalem asked of Paul, “the same which I also was forward to do” ([[Gal.2.10|Galatians 2:10]]).
God sent quail around Israel’s camp in the wilderness ([[Num.11.31|Numbers 11:31]]), and rained down manna, “bread from heaven” ([[Exod.16.4|Exodus 16:4]]).

modern:
This is the seventh of the Beatitudes, and seven was the number of perfection among the Hebrews. Perhaps the Savior put the peacemaker seventh on the list because he comes closest to the perfect person in Christ Jesus. Anyone who wants perfect blessedness, as far as it can be had on earth, must reach this seventh blessing and become a peacemaker.

The place of the text matters too. The verse before it speaks of the blessedness of “the pure in heart: for they shall see God.” It’s good to understand that we’re to be “first pure, then peaceable.” Our peaceableness must never be a deal with sin or a toleration of evil. We must set our faces like flint against everything opposed to God and his holiness. Once purity is settled in our souls, we can go on to peaceableness. The verse that follows seems to have been put there on purpose too. However peaceable we may be in this world, we’ll still be misrepresented and misunderstood. And no wonder, because even the Prince of Peace, by his very peacefulness, brought fire on the earth. Though he loved humanity and did no harm, he was “despised and rejected of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.” So that the peaceable in heart won’t be surprised when they meet enemies, the next verse adds, “Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” So peacemakers aren’t only declared blessed; they’re surrounded with blessings. Lord, give us grace to climb to this seventh Beatitude! Purify our minds, so that we may be “first pure, then peaceable,” and strengthen our souls, so that our peaceableness won’t lead us into cowardice and despair when we’re persecuted for your sake.

notes.note: The blessings that open the Sermon on the Mount, each starting “Blessed are…” ([[Matt.5.3-Matt.5.10|Matthew 5:3–10]]).

modern: *God’s fatherhood belongs equally to all his children.* Ah, Little-faith, you’ve often said, “Oh, if only I had Great-heart’s courage, so I could swing his sword and be as brave as he is! But I stumble at every straw, and a shadow scares me.” Listen, Little-faith. Great-heart is God’s child, and you’re God’s child too, and Great-heart isn’t one bit more God’s child than you are. Peter and Paul, the highly favored apostles, belonged to the family of the Most High, and so do you. The weak Christian is as much a child of God as the strong one.

All the names are in the same family register. One may have more grace than another, but God our heavenly Father has the same tender heart toward all of them. One may do mightier works and bring more glory to his Father, but the one whose name is least in the kingdom of heaven is as much God’s child as the one who stands among the King’s mighty men. Let this cheer and comfort us when we come near to God and say, “Our Father.”

Yet while we take comfort from knowing this, let’s not settle down content with weak faith, but ask, like the apostles, to have it increased. However feeble our faith is, if it’s real faith in Christ, we’ll reach heaven in the end. But we won’t honor our Master much along the way, and we won’t overflow with joy and peace. So if you want to live for Christ’s glory and be happy in his service, seek to be filled with the spirit of adoption more and more completely, until perfect love drives out fear.

modern:
Jesus loves his people in the same way the Father loves the Son. How does the Father love him? He loves him *without beginning*, and that’s how Jesus loves his people. “*I have loved thee with an everlasting love*.” You can trace the beginning of human love. You can easily find the start of your own love for Christ. But his love for us is a stream whose source is hidden in eternity. God the Father loves Jesus *without any change*. Christian, take comfort from this: there’s no change in Jesus Christ’s love for those who rest in him. Yesterday you were on top of Mount Tabor and you said, “He loves me.” Today you’re in the valley of humiliation, but he loves you just the same. On the hill Mizar and among the Hermons, you heard his voice speaking so sweetly with the dove’s notes of love. And now, on the sea, or even in the sea, when all his waves and breakers go over you, his heart is faithful to his ancient choice.

The Father loves the Son *without any end*, and that’s how the Son loves his people. Saint, you don’t need to fear the silver cord coming loose, because his love for you will never stop. Be confident that Christ will go with you right down to the grave, and lead you up again from it to the hills of heaven. What’s more, the Father loves the Son *without any measure*, and the Son gives the same measureless love to his chosen ones. The whole heart of Christ is given to his people. He “loved us and gave himself for us.” His is a love that passes knowledge. Ah, we really do have an unchanging Savior, a precious Savior, one who loves without measure, without change, without beginning and without end, just as the Father loves him! There’s plenty of food here for those who know how to digest it. May the Holy Spirit lead us into its richest parts!

modern:
Christian, take good care of your faith, because remember, *faith is the only way you can get blessings*. If we want blessings from God, nothing but faith can bring them down. Prayer can’t draw answers down from God’s throne unless it’s the earnest prayer of someone who believes. Faith is the angel messenger between the soul and the Lord Jesus in glory. Take that angel away, and we can neither send prayer up nor receive the answers. Faith is the telegraph wire linking earth and heaven, along which God’s messages of love fly so fast that before we call he answers, and while we’re still speaking he hears. But if that telegraph wire of faith is cut, how can we receive the promise? Am I in trouble? I can get help for trouble by faith. Am I battered by the enemy? My soul leans on her dear Refuge by faith. But take faith away, and I call to God in vain. There’s no road between my soul and heaven. In the depth of winter, faith is a road the horses of prayer can travel on, yes, and all the better for the biting frost. But block the road, and how can we reach the great King?

Faith links me with God. Faith clothes me with the power of God. Faith puts the almighty power of the Lord on my side. Faith brings every quality of God to my defense. It helps me defy the armies of hell. It makes me march in triumph over the necks of my enemies. But without faith, how can I receive anything from the Lord? Don’t let the one who wavers, who is like a wave of the sea, expect to receive anything from God! So, Christian, watch your faith carefully. With it you can win everything, however poor you are, but without it you can get nothing. “If thou canst believe, all things are possible to him that believeth.”

modern:
Whenever we have the privilege of eating the bread Jesus gives, we’re like Ruth: satisfied with the full, sweet meal. When Jesus is the host, no guest goes away from the table empty. Our *head* is satisfied with the precious truth Christ reveals. Our *heart* is content with Jesus as the altogether lovely object of its love. Our *hope* is satisfied, because whom do we have in heaven but Jesus? And our desire is filled, because what more could we want than “to know Christ and to be found in him”? Jesus fills our *conscience* until it’s at perfect peace, our *judgment* with the certainty of his teaching, our *memory* with what he has done, and our *imagination* with the prospect of what he is yet to do.

As Ruth “was sufficed, *and left*,” so it is with us. We’ve taken long drinks. We’ve thought we could take in all of Christ. But when we’ve done our best, we’ve had to leave a vast amount behind. We’ve sat at the table of the Lord’s love and said, “Nothing but the infinite can ever satisfy me. I’m such a great sinner that I must have infinite merit to wash my sin away.” But our sin has been taken away, and we’ve found there was merit to spare. Our hunger has been satisfied at the feast of holy love, and we’ve found there was plenty of spiritual food left over. There are sweet things in the Word of God we haven’t enjoyed yet, and have to leave for a while, because we’re like the disciples to whom Jesus said, “I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now.” Yes, there are graces we haven’t reached, places of fellowship closer to Christ we haven’t arrived at, and heights of communion our feet haven’t climbed. At every banquet of love there are many baskets of leftovers. Let’s praise the generosity of our glorious Boaz.

modern: This was a golden name the church of old used to give the Lord’s Anointed in her happiest moments. When the time of the singing of birds had come, and the voice of the turtledove was heard in her land, *her* love song was sweeter than either, as she sang, “*My beloved* is mine and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.” All through her Song of Songs she calls him by that delightful name, “My beloved!” Even in the long winter, when idol worship had withered the Lord’s garden, her prophets found room to put down the burden of the Lord for a little while and say, as Isaiah did, “Now will I sing to my well-beloved a song of my beloved touching his vineyard.” Though the saints had never seen his face, though he hadn’t yet become flesh or lived among us, and no one had yet seen his glory, he was still the consolation of Israel, the hope and joy of all the chosen, the “beloved” of all who were upright before the Most High. We, in the summer days of the church, also speak of Christ as our soul’s best beloved, and feel that he is very precious, the “chiefest among ten thousand, and the altogether lovely.” It’s so true that the church loves Jesus and claims him as her beloved that the apostle dares to challenge the whole universe to separate her from the love of Christ. He declares that persecution, distress, affliction, danger and the sword haven’t managed to do it. No, he joyfully boasts, “In all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.”
Oh, that we knew more of you, ever precious One!

modern:
What a golden example Christ gives his disciples! Few teachers could dare to say, “If you want to practice my teaching, copy my life.” But since the life of Jesus is the exact copy of perfect goodness, he can point to himself as the model of holiness as well as its teacher. The Christian should settle for nothing less than Christ as his model. In no situation should we be content unless we reflect the grace that was in him. As a husband, the Christian is to look at the portrait of Christ Jesus and paint from that original. The true Christian is to be the kind of husband Christ was to his church.

A husband’s love is *special*. The Lord Jesus has a particular affection for the church, set on her above the rest of humanity: “I pray for them, I pray not for the world.” The chosen church is heaven’s favorite, Christ’s treasure, the crown of his head, the bracelet on his arm, the breastplate over his heart, the very center and core of his love. A husband should love his wife with a *constant* love, because that’s how Jesus loves his church. His affection doesn’t vary. He may change in how he shows it, but the affection itself stays the same. A husband should love his wife with a *lasting* love, because nothing “shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.” A true husband loves his wife with a *heartfelt* love, warm and intense. It isn’t mere lip service. Ah, dear friends, what more could Christ have done to prove his love than he has done? Jesus has a *delighted love* for his bride. He values her love and takes sweet pleasure in her. Believer, you wonder at Jesus’ love; you admire it. *Are you copying it?* In your home life, is the rule and measure of your love “*even as Christ loved the church*”?
