modern:
Few shared in the sorrows of Gethsemane. Most of the disciples weren’t far enough along in grace to be let in to see the mysteries of “the agony.” Busy with the Passover feast in their own houses, they stand for the many who live on the letter of the gospel but are mere babies as to its spirit. Only twelve, no, only eleven, were given the privilege of entering Gethsemane and seeing “this great sight.” Of those eleven, eight were left at a distance. They had fellowship with him, but not the close kind that people greatly loved are let into. Only three specially favored ones could come near the curtain of our Lord’s mysterious sorrow, and even they mustn’t intrude behind that curtain. A stone’s throw had to be left between. He had to tread the winepress *alone*, and of the people there was to be no one with him.

Peter and the two sons of Zebedee stand for the few outstanding, experienced saints who can be written down as “fathers.” Having done business on great waters, they can in some degree measure the huge Atlantic waves of their Redeemer’s suffering. To some chosen spirits it’s given, for the good of others and to strengthen them for some future, special and tremendous battle, to enter the inner circle and hear the pleading of the suffering High Priest. They have fellowship with him in his sufferings and are made like him in his death. Yet even they can’t get into the secret places of the Savior’s sorrow. “Thine unknown sufferings” is the remarkable phrase of the Greek liturgy. There was an inner room in our Master’s grief, shut off from all human knowledge and fellowship. There Jesus is “*left alone*.” Here Jesus was more than ever an “Unspeakable gift!” Isn’t Watts right when he sings,

modern: If we’re tempted to boast of our abilities, the grandeur of nature can soon show us how puny we are. We can’t move the smallest of the twinkling stars, or put out even one of the beams of the morning. We talk about power, but the heavens laugh us to scorn. When the Pleiades shine out in spring with springtime joy, we can’t hold back their influence. And when Orion rules overhead and the year is bound in winter’s chains, we can’t loosen the icy bands. The seasons turn as God has appointed, and the whole human race can’t make any change in them. Lord, what is man?

In the spiritual world, as in the natural world, human power is limited on every side. When the Holy Spirit pours out his delights in the soul, no one can disturb them. All the cunning and spite of people can’t stop the warm, life-giving power of the Comforter. When he chooses to visit a church and revive it, the most determined enemies can’t resist the good work. They may mock it, but they can no more hold it back than they can push back the spring when the Pleiades rule the season. God wills it, and so it must be. On the other hand, if the Lord, in his sovereignty or his justice, binds a person so that their soul is in chains, who can set them free? Only he can take away the winter of spiritual death from a person or a people. He looses the bands of Orion, and no one but he.

What a blessing that he can do it! Oh, that he would do the wonder tonight! Lord, end my winter, and let my spring begin. With all my longing I can’t raise my soul out of her deadness and dullness, but all things are possible with you. I need heavenly influences, the clear shining of your love, the beams of your grace, the light of your face. These are the Pleiades to me. I suffer much from sin and temptation; these are my wintry signs, my terrible Orion. Lord, work wonders in me and for me. Amen.

modern: Our Savior’s prayer in his hour of trial has several features worth learning from. It was *lonely prayer*. He withdrew even from his three favorite disciples. Believer, pray much alone, especially in times of trial. Family prayer, prayer together with others, prayer in the church won’t be enough. These are very precious, but the finest beaten spice will smoke in your censer in your private devotions, where no ear hears but God’s.

It was *humble prayer*. Luke says he knelt, but another Gospel writer says he “fell on his face.” Then where must *your* place be, humble servant of the great Master? What dust and ashes should cover *your* head! Humility gives us a good foothold in prayer. There’s no hope of prevailing with God unless we bring ourselves low, so that he may lift us up in due time.

It was *a child’s prayer*. “Abba, Father.” You’ll find it a stronghold in the day of trial to plead that you are God’s adopted child. You have no rights as a subject; you’ve forfeited them by your treason. But nothing can forfeit a child’s right to a father’s protection. Don’t be afraid to say, “My Father, hear my cry.”

Notice that it was *persevering prayer*. He prayed three times. Don’t stop until you prevail. Be like the persistent widow, whose continual coming won what her first request couldn’t. Keep on in prayer, and watch in it with thanksgiving.

Last of all, *it was the prayer of resignation*. “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as thou wilt.” Yield, and God yields. Let it be as God wills, and God will decide what’s best. Be content to leave your prayer in his hands. He knows when to give, how to give, what to give and what to hold back. If you plead like this, earnestly and persistently, yet with humility and resignation, you will surely prevail.

modern:
Oh, death! Why do you touch the tree whose spreading branches give the weary rest? Why do you snatch away the excellent of the earth, in whom is all our delight? If you must use your axe, use it on the trees that bear no fruit; then you might be thanked. But why will you cut down the fine cedars of Lebanon? Oh, hold back your axe, and spare the righteous. But no, it can’t be. Death strikes the best of our friends. The most generous, the most prayerful, the most holy, the most devoted must die. And why? It’s because of Jesus’ prevailing prayer: “Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am.” It is *that* which carries them on eagle’s wings to heaven. Every time a believer rises from this earth to paradise, it’s an answer to Christ’s prayer.

A good old preacher remarks, “Many times Jesus and his people pull against one another in prayer. You bend your knee in prayer and say ‘Father, I will that thy saints be with me where *I* am’; Christ says, ‘Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where *I* am.’” So the disciple is at cross-purposes with his Lord. The soul can’t be in both places: the loved one can’t be with Christ and with you too. Now, which of the two pleading will win the day? Suppose you had the choice. Suppose the King stepped down from his throne and said, “Here are two people praying against each other. Which shall be answered?” Oh! I’m sure that, even if it were agony, you would jump to your feet and say, “Jesus, not my will, but thine be done.” You would give up your prayer for your loved one’s life, if you could take in the thought that Christ is praying the opposite way: “Father, I will that they also, whom thou hast given me, be with me where I am.” Lord, you shall have them. By faith we let them go.

modern:
The strain on our Lord’s mind from his struggle with temptation so forced his body into an unnatural state that his pores poured out great drops of blood, which fell down to the ground. This shows *how tremendous the weight of sin must have been*, when it could crush the Savior so that he dripped great drops of blood! This shows *the mighty power of his love*. Old Isaac Ambrose makes a very pretty observation: the gum that oozes from a tree without cutting is always the best. This precious camphire tree gave its sweetest spices when it was wounded under the knotted whips, and when it was pierced by the nails on the cross. But see, it gives its best spice when there’s no whip, no nail, no wound. This shows that *Christ’s sufferings were freely chosen*, since the blood flowed freely without a lance. No need to put on the leech or use the knife; it flows on its own. No need for the rulers to cry, “Spring up, O well”; it flows by itself in crimson torrents.

When people suffer great pain of mind, the blood seems to rush to the heart. The cheeks go pale; a fainting fit comes on; the blood has gone inward, as if to nourish the inner man while he passes through his trial. But see our Savior in his agony. He’s so completely forgetful of himself that instead of his agony driving his blood to the heart to nourish himself, it drives it outward to wet the earth. The agony of Christ, in pouring him out on the ground, pictures how full the offering was that he made for men.

Don’t we see how intense the wrestling must have been that he went through? And won’t we hear what it says *to us*? “Ye have not yet resisted unto blood, striving against sin.” Look at the great Apostle and High Priest of our profession, and sweat even to blood rather than give in to the great tempter of your souls.

modern:
But could the stones cry out? Certainly they could, if the One who opens the mouth of the mute told them to lift up their voice. And if they did speak, they’d have plenty to say in praise of the One who created them by the word of his power. They could praise the wisdom and power of their *Maker*, who called them into being. Shall *we* not speak well of him who made us new, and out of stones raised up children for Abraham? The old rocks could tell of chaos and order, and of God’s handiwork in the stages of creation’s drama. And can’t *we* talk of God’s decrees, of God’s great work in ancient times, of all he did for his church in the days of old?

If the stones spoke, they could tell of their *breaker*: how he took them from the quarry and made them fit for the temple. And can’t we tell of our glorious Breaker, who broke our hearts with the hammer of his word so that he could build us into his temple? If the stones cried out, they’d praise their *builder*, who polished them and shaped them after the likeness of a palace. And shall we not talk of our Architect and Builder, who has put us in our place in the temple of the living God? If the stones could cry out, they might have a long, long story to tell as a memorial, for many times a great stone has been rolled into place as a memorial before the Lord. We too can tell of Ebenezers, stones of help, pillars of remembrance.

The broken stones of the law cry out against us, but Christ himself, who rolled away the stone from the door of the tomb, speaks for us. The stones might well cry out, but we won’t let them. We’ll drown out their noise with ours. We’ll break out into sacred song, and bless the majesty of the Most High all our days, glorifying the One whom Jacob called the Shepherd and Stone of Israel.

modern:
Did this fear come from the hellish suggestion *that he was utterly forsaken*? There may be harder trials than this, but surely it’s *one* of the worst, to be utterly forsaken. “See,” said Satan, “you don’t have a friend anywhere! Your Father has shut up his tender compassion against you. Not one angel in his courts will stretch out a hand to help you. All heaven is turned against you; you’re left alone. Look at the companions you shared sweet counsel with. What are they worth? Son of Mary, see your brother James there, see your beloved disciple John, and your bold apostle Peter. Look how the cowards sleep while you suffer! Look! You have no friend left in heaven or earth. All hell is against you. I’ve stirred up my hellish den. I’ve sent my orders through every region, summoning every prince of darkness to attack you tonight. We’ll spare no arrows. We’ll use all our hellish might to overwhelm you. And what will you do, you lonely one?”

Maybe this was the temptation. We think it was, because the appearance of an angel strengthening him took that fear away. He was heard in that he feared: he was no longer alone; heaven was with him. Maybe this is why he came to his disciples three times, as Hart puts it:

He wanted to see for himself whether it was really true that everyone had forsaken him. He found them all asleep. But perhaps he got some faint comfort from the thought that they were sleeping not from treachery but from sorrow: the spirit indeed was willing, but the flesh was weak. In any case, he was heard in that he feared. Jesus was heard in his deepest grief; my soul, you will be heard too.

modern:
The Savior was “a man of sorrows,” but every thoughtful mind has discovered that deep down in his innermost soul he carried an endless treasury of refined and heavenly joy. Of all the human race, there was never a man with a deeper, purer or more lasting peace than our Lord Jesus Christ. “He was anointed with the oil of gladness above his fellows.” His boundless kindness must, by the very nature of things, have given him the deepest possible delight, for kindness is joy. There were a few remarkable times when this joy showed itself. “At that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” Christ had his songs, though it was night for him. Though his face was marred, and had lost the glow of earthly happiness, yet sometimes it lit up with a matchless splendor of unequaled satisfaction, as he thought of the reward to come, and in the middle of the congregation sang his praise to God.

In this, the Lord Jesus is a blessed picture of his church on earth. Right now the church expects to walk in sympathy with her Lord along a thorny road. Through much trouble she’s forcing her way to the crown. Bearing the cross is her task, and being scorned and treated as a stranger by her mother’s children is her lot. And yet the church has a deep well of joy that no one can drink from but her own children. There are stores of wine and oil and grain hidden in the middle of our Jerusalem, and on them the saints of God are always sustained and nourished. And sometimes, as in our Savior’s case, we have our seasons of intense delight, for “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of our God.” Exiles though we are, we rejoice in our King. Yes, in him we rejoice exceedingly, while in his name we set up our banners.

modern: “The kisses of an enemy are deceitful.” Let me be on my guard when the world puts on a loving face, because if it can, it’ll betray me as it did my Master, with a kiss. Whenever someone is about to stab religion, they usually claim to have great reverence for it. Let me beware of the smooth-faced hypocrisy that carries the armor for false teaching and unbelief. Knowing how deceitful unrighteousness is, let me be wise as a serpent to spot and avoid the enemy’s schemes. The young man without understanding was led astray by the kiss of the strange woman. May my soul be so graciously taught all through this day that “the much fair speech” of the world has no effect on me. Holy Spirit, don’t let me, a poor frail son of man, be betrayed with a kiss!

But what if I should be guilty of the same cursed sin as Judas, that son of perdition? I’ve been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus. I’m a member of his visible church. I sit at the communion table. All of these are so many kisses of my lips. Am I sincere in them? If not, I’m a contemptible traitor. Do I live in the world as carelessly as others do, and yet claim to be a follower of Jesus? Then I’m bound to expose religion to ridicule, and lead people to speak evil of the holy name I’m called by. Surely if I act this inconsistently I’m a Judas, and it would be better for me if I’d never been born. Dare I hope that I’m clear in this? Then, O Lord, keep me so. O Lord, make me sincere and true. Keep me from every false way. Never let me betray my Savior. I do love you, Jesus, and though I often grieve you, I still long to stay faithful even to death. O God, forbid that I should be a high-flying professing Christian, and then fall at last into the lake of fire, because I betrayed my Master with a kiss.

modern:
How constantly our Master used the title “Son of man”! If he had chosen, he could always have spoken of himself as the Son of God, the Everlasting Father, the Wonderful, the Counselor, the Prince of Peace. But look at the lowliness of Jesus! He prefers to call himself the Son of man. Let’s learn a lesson of humility from our Savior, and never chase after great titles or proud degrees.

There’s a far sweeter thought here, though. Jesus loved human nature so much that he delighted to honor it. And since it is a high honor, in fact the greatest dignity of humankind, that Jesus is the Son of man, he makes a habit of displaying this name. It’s as if he hangs royal stars on the chest of humanity, and shows the love of God to Abraham’s seed. *Son of man*: whenever he said that word, he shed a halo around the head of Adam’s children.

Yet there’s perhaps a more precious thought still. Jesus Christ called himself the Son of man to express his oneness and sympathy with his people. In this way he reminds us that he’s the one we can come to without fear. Since he is a man, we can take all our griefs and troubles to him, because he knows them by experience. Because he himself has suffered as the “Son of man,” he is able to help and comfort us. All hail, blessed Jesus! Because you are always using the sweet name that admits you are a brother and a close kinsman, it’s a dear sign to us of your grace, your humility, your love.

modern:
Notice, my soul, the care Jesus showed, even in his hour of trial, for the sheep of his hand! The ruling passion is strong in death. He gives himself up to the enemy, but he puts in a word of power to set his disciples free. As for himself, like a sheep before her shearers he is silent and doesn’t open his mouth; but for his disciples’ sake he speaks with almighty energy. Here is love: constant, self-forgetting, faithful love.

But isn’t there far more here than appears on the surface? Don’t we have the very soul and spirit of the atonement in these words? The Good Shepherd lays down his life for the sheep, and pleads that because of this they must go free. The Surety is bound, and justice demands that those he stands in for as a substitute should go their way. In the middle of Egypt’s slavery, that voice rings out as a word of power: “*Let these go their way*.” Out of the slavery of sin and Satan the redeemed must come. In every cell of the dungeons of Despair the sound echoes, “*Let these go their way*,” and out come Despondency and Much-afraid. Satan hears the well-known voice and lifts his foot from the neck of the fallen. Death hears it, and the grave opens her gates to let the dead rise. *Their way* is one of progress, holiness, triumph and glory, and no one will dare to stop them on it. No lion will be on their way, and no ravenous beast will go up on it. “The hind of the morning” has drawn the cruel hunters onto himself, and now the most timid deer of the field may graze in perfect peace among the lilies of his loves. The thundercloud has burst over the cross of Calvary, and the pilgrims of Zion will never be struck by the lightning bolts of vengeance. Come, my heart, rejoice in the safety your Redeemer has won for you, and bless his name all day, and every day.

modern:
If we’ve shared Jesus’ shame, we’ll share the brightness that will surround him when he appears again in glory. Dear friend, are you with Christ Jesus? Does a living union bind you to him? Then you’re with him today in his shame. You’ve taken up his cross and gone with him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. You will surely be with him when the cross is exchanged for the crown. But judge yourself this evening. If you’re not with him in the new birth, you won’t be with him when he comes in his glory. If you shrink back from the dark side of fellowship with him, you won’t understand its bright and happy time, when the King comes, and *all his holy angels with him*.

What! Are *angels with him*? And yet he didn’t take on the nature of angels; he took on the seed of Abraham. Are the holy angels *with him*? Come, my soul, if you really are his own dear one, you can’t be far from him. If his friends and his neighbors are called together to see his glory, what do you think, if you are married to him? Will you be kept at a distance? Though it’s a day of judgment, you can’t be far from that heart which has let angels into close friendship, but has let you into union.

Hasn’t he said to you, O my soul, “I will betroth thee unto me in righteousness, and in judgment, and in lovingkindness?” Haven’t his own lips said, “I am married unto thee, and my delight is in thee?” If the angels, who are only friends and neighbors, will be with him, it’s absolutely certain that his own dear Hephzibah, in whom is all his delight, will be near him and sit at his right hand. Here’s a morning star of hope for you, so bright that it may well light up the darkest and loneliest experience.

modern:
He never deserted them, but in cowardly fear for their lives they fled from him at the very start of his sufferings. This is just one example that shows how frail all believers are if left to themselves. They are only sheep at best, and they run when the wolf comes. They’d all been warned of the danger, and had promised to die rather than leave their Master. And yet they were seized with sudden panic and took to their heels.

It may be that I, at the start of this day, have braced my mind to bear a trial for the Lord’s sake, and I imagine I’m sure to show perfect faithfulness. But let me keep a very close watch on myself, in case, having the same evil heart of unbelief, I should turn away from my Lord as the apostles did. It’s one thing to promise, and quite another to perform. It would have been to their eternal honor to have stood bravely at Jesus’ side. They ran from honor. May I be kept from copying them! Where else could they have been as safe as near their Master, who could at once call for twelve legions of angels? They ran away from their true safety. O God, don’t let me play the fool too.

Divine grace can make the coward brave. The smoking flax can blaze up like fire on the altar when the Lord wills it. These same apostles, who were timid as hares, grew bold as lions after the Spirit had come down on them. In the same way the Holy Spirit can make my faint-hearted spirit brave to confess my Lord and witness for his truth.

What anguish must have filled the Savior as he saw his friends so faithless! This was one bitter ingredient in his cup. But that cup is drained dry; don’t let me put another drop in it. If I forsake my Lord, I’ll crucify him all over again, and put him to an open shame. Keep me, O blessed Spirit, from such a shameful end.

modern:
This woman found comfort in her misery by thinking *great thoughts of Christ*. The Master had talked about the children’s bread. “Now,” she reasoned, “since you are the Master of the table of grace, I know you’re a generous host, and there’s sure to be plenty of bread on your table. There’ll be so much for the children that there will be crumbs to throw on the floor for the dogs, and the children won’t go short because the dogs are fed.” She thought of him as one who kept so good a table that all she needed would be only a crumb by comparison. Yet remember, what she wanted was to have the devil driven out of her daughter. It was a very great thing to her, but she had such a high opinion of Christ that she said, “It’s nothing to him. It’s only a crumb for Christ to give.” This is the royal road to comfort.

Great thoughts of your sin alone will drive you to despair, but great thoughts of Christ will steer you into the harbor of peace. “My sins are many, but oh! it’s nothing to Jesus to take them all away. The weight of my guilt presses me down as a giant’s foot would crush a worm, but it’s no more than a grain of dust to him, because he has already carried its curse in his own body on the tree. It will be only a small thing for him to give me full forgiveness, though it will be an infinite blessing for me to receive it.” The woman opens her soul’s mouth very wide, expecting great things of Jesus, and he fills it with his love. Dear reader, do the same.

She admitted what Christ laid at her door, but she held tight to him, and drew arguments even out of his hard words. She believed great things of him, and so she overcame him. *She won the victory by believing in him.* Her case is an example of faith that prevails, and if we want to conquer like her, we must copy her tactics.

modern: The love of Christ, in its sweetness, its fullness, its greatness and its faithfulness, goes beyond all human understanding. Where will language be found to describe his matchless, unequaled love toward the children of men? It’s so vast and boundless that, as the swallow only skims the water and doesn’t dive into its depths, all our words only touch the surface, while depths beyond measure lie below. Well might the poet say,

for this love of Christ really is measureless and fathomless; no one can reach it. Before we can have any right idea of the love of Jesus, we must understand the glory he had before, in all its height of majesty, and his coming in the flesh on the earth, in all its depths of shame. But who can tell us the majesty of Christ? When he was enthroned in the highest heavens he was very God of very God. By him the heavens were made, and all their hosts. His own almighty arm held up the spheres. The praises of cherubim and seraphim surrounded him without end. The full chorus of the hallelujahs of the universe flowed without ceasing to the foot of his throne. He reigned supreme over all his creatures, God over all, blessed forever. Who can tell the height of his glory then?

And who, on the other hand, can tell how low he came down? To be a man was something; to be a man of sorrows was far more. To bleed, and die, and suffer: these were much for him who was the Son of God. But to suffer such unequaled agony, to endure a death of shame and to be deserted by his Father, this is a depth of stooping love which the most inspired mind must utterly fail to fathom. Here is love! And truly it is love that “passeth knowledge.” Oh, let this love fill our hearts with adoring gratitude, and lead us to show its power in practical ways.

notes.note: Goes beyond. Paul prays that we may “know the love of Christ, which passeth knowledge” ([[Eph.3.19|Ephesians 3:19]]).

modern:
The merits of our great Redeemer are a sweet fragrance to the Most High. Whether we speak of Christ’s active or passive righteousness, the fragrance is the same. There was a sweet fragrance in his active life, by which he honored the law of God and made every command glitter like a precious jewel in the pure setting of his own person. So too with his passive obedience, when with uncomplaining submission he endured hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and at last sweated great drops of blood in Gethsemane, gave his back to the beaters and his cheeks to those who pulled out the hair, and was fastened to the cruel wood, so that he might suffer the wrath of God on our behalf. These two things are sweet before the Most High. And for the sake of his doing and his dying, his sufferings in our place and his obedience on our behalf, the Lord our God accepts us.

What preciousness there must be in him, to make up for our lack of it! What a sweet fragrance, to take away our foul smell! What cleansing power in his blood, to take away sin like ours! And what glory in his righteousness, to make such unacceptable creatures accepted in the Beloved! Notice, believer, how sure and unchanging our acceptance must be, since it is *in him*! Make sure you never doubt that you’re accepted in Jesus. You can’t be accepted without Christ; but once you’ve received his merit, you can’t be unaccepted. In spite of all your doubts and fears and sins, Jehovah’s gracious eye never looks on you in anger. Though he sees sin in you, in yourself, yet when he looks at you through Christ, he sees no sin. You are always accepted in Christ, always blessed and dear to the Father’s heart. So lift up a song. And as you see the smoking incense of the Savior’s merit rising this evening before the sapphire throne, let the incense of your praise go up too.

notes.note: A pleasing smell, the old word for a sacrifice God accepts. Christ “gave himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour” ([[Eph.5.2|Ephesians 5:2]]).

modern:
We’re told that the Captain of our salvation was made perfect through suffering. So we who are sinful, and far from perfect, mustn’t be surprised if we’re called to go through suffering too. Shall the head be crowned with thorns, and the other members of the body be rocked on the soft lap of ease? Must Christ pass through seas of his own blood to win the crown, and are we to walk to heaven with dry feet in silver slippers? No. Our Master’s experience teaches us that suffering is necessary, and the true-born child of God must not, and would not, escape it even if he could.

But there’s one very comforting thought in the fact of Christ’s “being made perfect through suffering”: it means he can have complete sympathy with us. “He is not an high priest that cannot be touched with the feeling of our infirmities.” In this sympathy of Christ we find a power that holds us up. One of the early martyrs said, “I can bear it all, for Jesus suffered, and he suffers in me now; he sympathizes with me, and this makes me strong.” Believer, hold on to this thought in all times of agony. Let the thought of Jesus strengthen you as you follow in his steps. Find sweet support in his sympathy, and remember that to suffer is an honorable thing; to suffer for Christ is glory. The apostles rejoiced that they were counted worthy to do this. Just as far as the Lord gives us grace to suffer *for* Christ, to suffer *with* Christ, just so far he honors us. A Christian’s jewels are his afflictions. The crown jewels of the kings whom God has anointed are their troubles, their sorrows and their griefs. So let’s not run from being honored. Let’s not turn aside from being lifted up. Griefs exalt us, and troubles lift us up. “If we suffer, we shall also reign with him.”

notes.note: “It became him… to make the captain of their salvation perfect through sufferings” ([[Heb.2.10|Hebrews 2:10]]).

modern:
Prayer sometimes waits, like a petitioner at the gate, until the King comes out to fill her lap with the blessings she’s asking for. When the Lord has given great faith, he has been known to test it by long delays. He has let his servants’ voices echo back in their ears as if from a sky of brass. They’ve knocked at the golden gate, but it has stayed shut, as though rusted on its hinges. Like Jeremiah, they’ve cried, “Thou hast covered thyself with a cloud, that our prayer should not pass through.” In this way true saints have gone on long in patient waiting without an answer. It wasn’t because their prayers weren’t fervent, or because they weren’t accepted, but because it pleased him who is Sovereign, and who gives as he pleases. If it pleases him to tell our patience to exercise itself, shall he not do as he wants with his own? Beggars can’t be choosers, whether about time, place or form.

But we must be careful not to take delays in prayer for denials. God’s long-dated bills will be paid on the day they fall due. We mustn’t let Satan shake our confidence in the God of truth by pointing to our unanswered prayers. Unanswered requests are not unheard. God keeps a file for our prayers. They aren’t blown away by the wind; they’re stored up in the King’s archives. There is a register in the court of heaven where every prayer is recorded. Tested believer, your Lord has a bottle for your tears, where the costly drops of holy grief are kept, and a book where your holy groanings are counted. Before long, your request will win through. Can’t you be content to wait a little? Won’t your Lord’s time be better than your time? Before long he will appear and comfort you, to your soul’s joy, and make you put away the sackcloth and ashes of long waiting, and put on the scarlet and fine linen of full fruition.

modern:
Why did Jesus let himself be enrolled among sinners? This wonderful condescension was justified by many powerful reasons. *In that character he could all the better become their advocate*. In some trials the lawyer is identified with the client, so that in the eye of the law they can’t be looked at apart from one another. Now, when the sinner is brought to the bar, Jesus appears there himself. *He* stands to answer the accusation. He points to his side, his hands, his feet, and challenges Justice to bring anything against the sinners he represents. He pleads his blood, and pleads so triumphantly, being numbered with them and having a part with them, that the Judge proclaims, “Let them go their way; deliver them from going down into the pit, for he hath found a ransom.”

Our Lord Jesus was numbered with the transgressors so that they might *feel their hearts drawn toward him*. Who can be afraid of someone written on the same list as we are? Surely we may come boldly to him and confess our guilt. He who is numbered with us can’t condemn us. Wasn’t he put down on the transgressors’ list *so that we might be written in the red roll of the saints*? He was holy, and written among the holy; we were guilty, and numbered among the guilty. He moves his name from that list to this black indictment, and our names are taken from the indictment and written in the roll of acceptance, for there is a complete exchange made between Jesus and his people. Jesus has taken all our estate of misery and sin, and all that Jesus has comes to us. His righteousness, his blood and everything he has, he gives us as our dowry. Rejoice, believer, in your union with him who was numbered among the transgressors; and prove that you are truly saved by being plainly numbered with those who are new creatures in him.

notes.note: Counted among the lawbreakers. Fulfilled when Jesus was crucified between two thieves ([[Mark.15.27-Mark.15.28|Mark 15:27–28]]).
Stooping down from a high position, in the good sense, without today’s sense of looking down on someone.

modern:
A wife who dearly loves her absent husband longs for him to come back. A long separation from him is half a death to her spirit. And so it is with souls who love the Savior much: they *must* see his face. They can’t bear for him to be away on the mountains of Bether, no longer holding fellowship with them. A reproachful glance, a raised finger, will grieve loving children who are afraid of offending their tender father and are only happy in his smile. Dear friend, it was like that with you once. A text of Scripture, a warning, a touch of the rod of affliction, and you went to your Father’s feet, crying, “Show me wherefore thou contendest with me?” Is it like that now? Are you content to follow Jesus at a distance? Can you think of your fellowship with Christ being broken off without alarm? Can you bear to have your Beloved walking against you, because you walk against him? Have your sins come between you and your God, and is your heart at rest?

Oh, let me warn you lovingly, for it’s a grievous thing when we can live contentedly without the present enjoyment of the Savior’s face. *Let’s work at feeling what an evil thing this is*: little love for our own dying Savior, little joy in our precious Jesus, little fellowship with the Beloved! Keep a true Lent in your souls, while you sorrow over your hardness of heart. But don’t stop at sorrow! Remember where you first received salvation. *Go at once to the cross*. There, and only there, can your spirit be made alive again. No matter how hard, how numb, how dead we may have become, let’s go again in all the rags and poverty and filth of our natural condition. Let’s cling to that cross. Let’s look into those weary eyes. Let’s bathe in that fountain filled with blood. This will bring back our first love; this will restore the simplicity of our faith and the tenderness of our heart.

modern: Pilate handed our Lord over to the lictors to be scourged. The Roman scourge was a most dreadful instrument of torture. It was made of the sinews of oxen, with sharp bones twisted in here and there among the sinews, so that every time the lash came down these pieces of bone tore fearful wounds and ripped the flesh from the bone. No doubt the Savior was tied to the pillar and beaten like this. He had been beaten before, but this beating by the Roman lictors was probably the most severe of all his floggings. My soul, stand here and weep over his poor battered body.

Believer in Jesus, can you look at him without tears, as he stands before you, the mirror of agonizing love? He is at once as fair as the lily for innocence and as red as the rose with the crimson of his own blood. As we feel the sure and blessed healing his stripes have worked in us, doesn’t our heart melt at once with love and grief? If we have ever loved our Lord Jesus, surely we must feel that love glowing now within our hearts.

We would gladly go to our rooms and weep; but since our business calls us away, we’ll first pray our Beloved to print the image of his bleeding self on the tablets of our hearts all through the day. And at nightfall we’ll come back to talk with him, and grieve that our sin should have cost him so dearly.

modern:
If a woman’s love for her dead sons could make her keep up her mournful watch for so long, shall we grow tired of thinking about the sufferings of our blessed Lord? She drove away the birds of prey; shall we not chase out of our meditations the worldly and sinful thoughts that defile both our minds and the sacred themes we’re thinking about? Away, you birds of evil wing! Leave the sacrifice alone! She bore the heat of summer, the night dews and the rains, unsheltered and alone. Sleep was driven from her weeping eyes: her heart was too full for sleep. See how she loved her children! Shall Rizpah endure like this, and shall we flinch at the first little inconvenience or trial? Are we such cowards that we can’t bear to suffer with our Lord? She chased away even the wild beasts, with courage unusual in her sex; and won’t we be ready to face every enemy for Jesus’ sake?

These children of hers were killed by other hands than hers, and yet she wept and watched. What ought we to do, who by our sins have crucified our Lord? Our debts to him are boundless; our love should be fervent and our repentance thorough. To watch with Jesus should be our business, to protect his honor our work, to stay by his cross our comfort. Those ghastly bodies might well have frightened Rizpah, especially at night; but in our Lord, at the foot of whose cross we are sitting, there is nothing repulsive, but everything attractive. Never was living beauty so enchanting as a dying Savior. Jesus, we will watch with you a while longer; graciously unveil yourself to us. Then we won’t sit beneath sackcloth, but in a royal pavilion.
